extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for distinguishing and assessing inductive reasoning, including what counts as induction vs mere description (colligation), the role of concept-formation, and the epistemic grounds (uniformity of nature) required for generalization from experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish description (colligation) from induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Confounding a mere description of a set of observed phenomena with an induction is an error. Colligation (bringing observations together under a general expression) is often not an inductive act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the navigator who, after coasting, ‘pronounces it an island’ — this is a summary of observed facts, not an inference of something unobserved; Kepler's expressing observed planetary places by the conception of an ellipse is of the same sort. Mill: 'That the land in question is an island, is not an inference from the partial facts... it is the facts themselves; it is a summary of those facts.' Distinguish the act of describing a whole from inferring a new, unobserved general truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction properly so called = generalization from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction consists in inferring from some individual instances in which a phenomenon is observed to occur, that it occurs in all instances of a certain class (those which resemble the former in the material circumstances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Mill's summary: 'INDUCTION properly so called... may, then, be summarily defined as Generalization from Experience.' Practical application requires specifying what counts as the relevant class and its material circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction is for explanation and prediction, not mere description
rubrics_metrics.description: The name 'induction' properly belongs to operations concerned with explanation or prediction; mere description (colligation) does not qualify as induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill: 'The philosophic study of facts may be undertaken for three different purposes: the simple description of the facts; their explanation; or their prediction... To the first of these the name of Induction does not properly belong: to the other two it does.' Use test: does the generalization increase explanatory or predictive power? If not, it's only description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction presupposes the uniformity of nature (the fundamental axiom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction implicitly assumes that there are parallel cases in nature — that what happens once will, under sufficient similarity of circumstances, happen again and always; this uniformity is the warrant for inference from experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill: 'Whatever be the most proper mode of expressing it, the proposition that the course of nature is uniform, is the fundamental principle, or general axiom, of Induction.' Note: Mill also stresses that this axiom itself is not an a priori truth but is itself an induction (see separate criterion). When structuring inductive arguments, the suppressed major premise corresponds to this axiom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptions used to colligate must correspond to properties in the facts
rubrics_metrics.description: A conception introduced to connect facts must be a conception of something which really is in the facts themselves — a property they actually possess and which would be manifest to our senses under appropriate conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill's point: though the conception 'is not in the facts, but in our mind, it must be a conception of something which really is in the facts.' Example: Kepler's ellipse corresponds to an actual property of planetary motion that would be visible given adequate observation; avoid inventing purely mental connections that lack grounding in the phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of conceptions is tentative and requires disciplined knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of selecting a conception to colligate facts consists of tentative successive guesses; many are rejected until a fit conception is found. Successful guesses are 'skilful' and rest on knowledge and scientific discipline, not luck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill: Kepler 'tried nineteen other imaginary paths' before the ellipse; 'the successful hypothesis, although a guess, ought not to be called a lucky, but a skilful guess.' Expect hypothesis-testing, iterative trial and expert judgment in forming general descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction must add predictive power to be genuine
rubrics_metrics.description: The true test of a new general truth (an induction) is that it adds to the power of prediction which was previously possessed; mere new descriptions add nothing to prediction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill: 'which is the true test of a new general truth) add anything to the power of prediction which they already possessed.' Example: Kepler's descriptive ellipse did not itself increase predictive power until induction about central force (gravitation) was made; when assessing a claim label it induction only if it extends prediction/explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colligation is a necessary preparation for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Before induction can be attempted, detached observations must be connected together by general descriptions (colligation) to provide a basis for inferring more general laws, especially for phenomena observable only piecemeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill: 'Induction always presupposes... that the results of these observations are... connected together by general descriptions, enabling the mind to represent to itself as wholes whatever phenomena are capable of being so represented.' In practice, assemble and summarize observations coherently before generalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: The connecting character must be real in the facts (avoid hypothesis-for-connection fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not enough that a conception connects observations; the connecting link must be some character which really exists in the facts and would manifest itself under proper conditions; otherwise one substitutes hypothesis for proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill warns: 'To suppose... that nothing more is required from the conception than that it shall serve to connect the observations, would be to substitute hypothesis for theory and imagination for proof.' Demand empirical evidence that the proposed connecting character is present in the phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction requires specifying material vs immaterial circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction infers that a phenomenon occurs in all instances which resemble the observed ones 'in what are regarded as the material circumstances'; identifying which circumstances are material is essential but nontrivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill: 'In what way the material circumstances are to be distinguished from those which are immaterial... we are not yet ready to point out.' When formulating generalizations, explicitly justify why certain conditions are treated as relevant (material) and others not.

rubrics_metrics.name: The uniformity-of-nature principle is itself the result of induction (not purely a priori)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although often stated as a fundamental axiom, the proposition that the course of nature is uniform should itself be regarded as a generalization from experience, and hence is not a primitive, self-evident ground for all inductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill: 'I hold it to be itself a generalization from experience.' He argues that it is one of the later and less obvious inductions to be established; thus be cautious in treating uniformity as an unquestioned, a priori premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every induction can be formulated as a syllogism with a suppressed major, but that major must be justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Any inductive inference can be cast into syllogistic form by supplying a major premise (the general law/uniformity), but where does that major come from? Its justification is not resolved by mere syllogistic recasting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill: 'Archbishop Whately... concludes that Induction itself is but a peculiar case of ratiocination... Our inquiries have led us to a directly opposite result.' Use syllogistic formalization for clarity, but do not assume the legitimacy of the major premise without independent empirical/inductive support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different colligations/descriptions can all be correct while conflicting inductions cannot
rubrics_metrics.description: Successive general expressions used as descriptions (colligations) may be all true 'as far as they go' given observational limits; however, conflicting explanations or inductions are not all true — only one (if any) can be correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill: historical example of circular theories, epicycles, and the elliptical theory — 'Different descriptions, therefore, may be all true: but not, surely, different explanations.' When evaluating competing claims, recognize that descriptive approximations can coexist usefully, but explanatory/predictive claims are mutually exclusive and require stronger testing.
